title: UK interest rate rise: what’s changed in the last decade?

breadcrumb.text: UK interest rate rise: what’s changed in the last decade?

body.text: 2 November 2017

Concerns about [“inflation over target”](https://www.cnbc.com/2017/10/13/cnbc-exclusive-transcript-bank-of-england-governor-mark-carney-speaks-with-cnbcs-steve-liesman-on-power-lunch-today.html)1 and ["limited" slack in the economy](http://www.bankofengland.co.uk/publications/Pages/news/2017/007.aspx) have prompted the Bank of England to raise interest rates for the first time in more than a decade.
At noon today (2 November 2017), the Bank’s Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) voted 7-2 in favour of raising the interest rate to 0.5%, from a record low of 0.25%.

The majority of the MPC agreed that now was the right time to raise interest rates [“to return inflation sustainably to the target](http://www.bankofengland.co.uk/publications/Pages/news/2017/007.aspx)”.

But the Committee acknowledged that "uncertainties associated with Brexit are weighing on domestic activity". Some economists, including former MPC member David Blanchflower, had [warned](https://www.theguardian.com/business/2017/sep/26/should-interest-rates-go-up-as-brexit-approaches-experts-debate-the-data) against an interest rate rise.

body.h3: What’s changed since the last interest rate rise?
body.text: What’s changed since the last interest rate rise?

body.h3: What’s changed since the last interest rate rise?
body.text: The last time we saw a rise in the interest rate was 5 July 2007. To put that into context, Tony Blair had recently resigned as Prime Minister and the first iPhone had just been released.

body.h3: What’s changed since the last interest rate rise?
body.text: On that day, the Bank voted for a higher interest rate against a backdrop of a [“strong global economy”](http://www.bankofengland.co.uk/publications/minutes/Documents/mpc/pdf/2007/mpc0707.pdf). The rate had risen twice that year already and there was little sign of the impending financial crisis.

body.h3: What’s changed since the last interest rate rise?
body.text: But between the last interest rate rise and today, the MPC had met 118 times and decided against raising interest rates on every occasion.

body.h3: What’s changed since the last interest rate rise?
body.text: When setting interest rates, the MPC considers many factors including debt, savings, inflation, economic growth, employment and wages. They’ll also look at conditions in economies and financial markets worldwide.

body.h3: What’s changed since the last interest rate rise?
body.text: So how similar is the situation today compared with 2007? We’ve gathered some of the main indicators and compared the latest data points with those that were available on 5 July 2007 - when the Bank last chose to raise the interest rate.

body.h3: Why has the interest rate stayed so low for so long?
body.text: Why has the interest rate stayed so low for so long?

body.h3: Why has the interest rate stayed so low for so long?
body.text: After rising to 5.75% in July 2007, the Bank of England base rate was subsequently cut nine times in the next two years as the financial crisis took effect.

body.h3: Why has the interest rate stayed so low for so long?
body.text: It reached a record low of 0.5% in March 2009 and remained at that level, partly because of the long-lasting impact of the crisis, before dropping again to 0.25% in August 2016.

body.text: But the general downward trend in interest rates goes back further than the last decade. Less than 30 years ago, the base rate was close to 15%.

body.h3: The interest rate has fallen substantially in the last 30 years
body.text: Despite today's rise, we're unlikely to see a substantial reversal to that trend - Mr Carney has said that any increases to the rate will be [“gradual” and “limited”](http://www.bbc.co.uk/news/business-41307167).
